strategyChanges.title: Final-position verification
strategyChanges.target: Missing a final king recapture or the remaining defender
strategyChanges.method: Revisit a known exchange, then test one short alternative and return to the benchmark.
strategyChanges.excerpt:
## Trial 4: final-position verification in forcing sequences

Learning period: revisit benchmark 3 after 22...Rc8 (ply 44), a remembered position. Check the resulting occupied squares and the defending piece after every capture, including a king recapture. A check is not mate unless every king destination, capture of the checking piece, and available block has been examined.

My own proposed correction is 23.Qxf6+ rather than sacrificing the rook on e8. It preserves the rook as a defender. Its consequences will be tested with a short recorded skill-5 drill, without requesting analysis. Next transfer test is benchmark 4; the first aggregate checkpoint remains six scored games.

Observable result: verify the drill's actual outcome, then avoid a queen or rook loss from a final king recapture in new play. No claim that a memorized drill alone demonstrates learning transfer.

### Trial 4 drill outcome

Practice 2 ended in checkmate after 23.Qxf6+ Kd7 24.Qe7#, three new plies, no illegal attempts. The rook on e6 protected the queen on e7. The referee verified the outcome; no engine analysis or advice was requested. This corrects the remembered example but does not yet show transfer.

After three scored benchmarks, the referee reports Elo 2070 with 95% credible interval 1110–3350, based on one calibrated win and excluding the two full-strength losses. This is a very small sample, conditional on nominal engine anchors and estimator assumptions, not a human rating.

Decision for benchmark 4: retain the correction's principle—explicitly verify the defender remaining in the final position—and watch the origin-square defenses. Next aggregate evaluation remains six scored benchmarks.

strategyChanges.target: Pawn breaks enabling supported queen checks
strategyChanges.method: Retain f7 when possible and verify occupied king-flight squares.
strategyChanges.excerpt: Trial 34 for benchmark 30: as Black, use c6/d5 against e4, with Bf5 and h6 if the actual opening permits; use e6/d5 development against other starts. Retain f7 unless an immediate concrete threat requires moving it, and preserve actual king flights rather than merely vacating f8 while occupying e7. Game 28's f6 enabled exf6 and a supported queen mate. Neither this pawn policy nor the opening choice has established transfer. Next aggregate checkpoint: immediately after benchmark 30.

strategyChanges.method: Return to 1.e4, prioritize ordinary development, and name the moving piece's former defense.
strategyChanges.excerpt: Trial 36 for benchmark 31: switch White's initial move to e4 and prioritize ordinary development, castling, and maintaining cheap pawn/minor-piece defenders. Before moving a defender, explicitly name the piece or pawn whose guard it removes, using the actual board. Before a queen exchange, check the opponent's immediate knight checks and their targets. This is a process and opening change together, so causal conclusions will be limited. Next aggregate evaluation after game 36; finish every measured game before a drill or study period.

limitations: The final completed game may have notes written afterward, absent from its start snapshot.
Declarations and short local event studies do not identify causal effects.
Two-rotation local windows overlap between nearby interventions and are exploratory.
